summary: High, cold plateau country beyond Jenolan Caves, where the sheer cliffs of Kanangra Walls drop into the gorge of Kanangra Deep and Mount Cloudmaker rises beyond. Part of the Greater Blue Mountains World Heritage Area, the park is quieter and wilder than its famous neighbour. Short walks lead to the Walls and to Kalang Falls, and free campsites sit among snow gums by the Boyd River.
story: Kanangra-Boyd lies on the high Boyd Plateau south-west of the Blue Mountains. Its eastern edge breaks off in cliffs: Kanangra Walls, Thurat Spires and the deep gorge of Kanangra Deep, with the Kalang, Kanangra and Morong waterfalls pouring off the plateau. The Kanangra, Jenolan, Coxs and Kowmung rivers drain the park into Lake Burragorang, the main store of Sydney's drinking water, and parts of the Kowmung are a declared wild river in near-pristine condition. There are karst landforms too, to be explored only by those with caving experience.

Height and exposure shape the plant life. Heath and mallee hold the wind-blasted tops, tall snow gum forest grows in the shelter, and Australian red cedar, one of the country's few native deciduous trees, grows in the gorges. The yellow Kanangra wattle grows only along the rivers and flowers in late winter and early spring. Red-necked wallabies, echidnas, wombats and lyrebirds are common, the spotted-tailed quoll survives here as a vulnerable species, and 195 bird species have been recorded, flame robins among them.

The park lies in the traditional Country of several Aboriginal language groups, among them the Gundungurra, Dharug, Wiradjuri, Dharawal and Darkinjung peoples. NPWS understands most of it to be Gundungurra and Dharug Country. Rock shelters, stone tools and artwork across the wider Greater Blue Mountains record a human presence going back at least 22,000 years. Since 2015 an Indigenous Land Use Agreement has recognised the Gundungurra People's custodianship of their Country, which takes in this park.

Before it was protected, the area was threatened by logging and by lime extraction. A five-year conservation effort followed. Kanangra-Boyd National Park was first reserved on 3 December 1969. It now covers about 74,713 hectares, much of it the Kanangra-Boyd wilderness area. In 2000 it became part of the Greater Blue Mountains Area World Heritage property, and in the summer of 2019–20 it was caught in bushfires of unprecedented extent and intensity.
howItWorks: Kanangra-Boyd is run by the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) from its Oberon office, under one plan of management with Blue Mountains National Park. The park is always open, but it may close in poor weather or high fire danger. NPWS lists it among NSW's fee-collecting parks, but says entry fees are under review and none is being collected. If you visit fee-collecting parks elsewhere, the All Parks Pass covers vehicle entry to every one of them in NSW, including Kosciuszko, for $190 a year. The Multi Park Pass covers all of them except Kosciuszko for $65. These prices were listed by NPWS in November 2026.

Boyd River and Dingo Dell campgrounds have no camping fee, but you book a site with NPWS online or on 1300 072 757, and a $6 booking fee applies. Both have toilets, picnic tables and barbecues; bring your own firewood. The campgrounds are remote, so arrive well prepared. Much of the park is declared wilderness, where there are few formed trails, group sizes are limited and horse riding is not allowed. Canyoning in the warmer months is popular, and the canyons here are larger, waterfall-type descents than the slot canyons of the Blue Mountains.

Bushfire season runs from October to March. On total fire ban days, usually declared around 5 pm the day before, all campfires and wood or solid-fuel barbecues are prohibited in NSW parks, as are liquid-fuel stoves, and visitor-owned gas and electric cookers are generally prohibited. NPWS can also declare a park fire ban or close the park when the fire risk is high. Mobile reception is limited across the park.

weather: Kanangra-Boyd is high and cold. Summer days average 10°C to 23°C, and the hottest on record reached only 34.5°C; it is the best season for camping, canyoning and wildlife. Winter averages −2°C to 10°C, with a record low of −10.1°C, and snow is possible. Day walks and mountain biking suit that season best, and the Kanangra wattle flowers yellow along the rivers in late winter. Spring brings comfortable temperatures for walking. June is usually the wettest month and March the driest.
directions: From Katoomba, drive west on the Great Western Highway through Mount Victoria and Hartley, turn left onto Jenolan Caves Road, and continue through Jenolan Caves. The main park entrance is 3 kilometres beyond the caves. Katoomba is about 79 kilometres away, and Kanangra is about 180 kilometres from Sydney. From Oberon, 24 kilometres away, take Ross Street off the main street and follow the signs for Jenolan Caves and the park. There is no public transport into the main section of the park, though a daily bus runs from Katoomba to Jenolan Caves.

chronology.text: Aboriginal people are living in the Greater Blue Mountains, as excavations at Kings Tableland show.
Kanangra-Boyd National Park is first reserved on 3 December.
The park is inscribed as part of the Greater Blue Mountains Area World Heritage property.
The Gundungurra Indigenous Land Use Agreement is registered, covering parts of the park.
Unprecedented bushfires burn across the Greater Blue Mountains.

safety: Mobile reception is limited. Download the Emergency Plus app before you go, and leave your plans with someone; for walks into the wilderness carry a personal locator beacon.
Keep well back from the edges at Kanangra Walls: the drops into Kanangra Deep are sheer.
The plateau is cold: winter nights fall well below freezing and snow is possible. Bring warm clothing even in summer.
Caving and canyoning here are for experienced, properly equipped parties only.
Check NPWS alerts and the Rural Fire Service before you go: the park may close on days of high fire danger.
regulations: No pets or domestic animals, except certified assistance animals.
No smoking: NSW national parks are smoke-free.
No campfires or wood barbecues during total fire bans or park fire bans; bring your own firewood at other times.
Horse riding is not permitted in wilderness areas, and cycling there is limited to designated trails.
